transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. 

Um, well, I'm an auditor, and what finally pushed me to make this appointment is that I'm having a lot of trouble finishing tasks I start at work. Like, I'll start working on follow-up items after my audits, or after mentorship events, and I have every intention of finishing them right then and there. But then I'll find out, you know, days later, that the final email, or a review note, or some form just never actually got done. It's becoming a real problem.
Have you struggled with this difficulty in finishing tasks your entire life, or is this a relatively new development?

It's definitely not a new thing. I've struggled with it my entire life, really. 

Um, even back in elementary school, my report cards would always say that I was bright, but that I lost assignments, or I rushed past small details. They also mentioned I talked out of turn a lot and constantly needed reminders to actually finish my work. My mother actually still jokes about it—she says I could easily ace a test, but then completely forget to turn in the project that was sitting right there in my backpack. So, yeah, it's been an ongoing issue.
Looking back at your childhood, would you say that you were frequently described as being constantly on the go or driven by a motor?

Yeah, definitely. I was always moving as a kid. And honestly, it hasn't really changed. Even now, um, on weekends I'll tell my husband that I'm just going to take it easy and rest. But then I end up bouncing from starting the laundry, to checking my email, to going for a run, to doing some volunteer planning... I just keep going from one thing to the next, and I don't really stop until I'm completely exhausted.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others while they are speaking or acting on impulses before thinking about the consequences?

Yes, I do that a lot. I catch myself jumping into conversations before people are even finished talking. It happens a lot at work, especially with the junior auditors. An answer or an idea will just pop into my head and it feels so urgent that I just blurt it out before I can even stop myself.

Looking back at your childhood, did you have significant difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or activities, such as frequently making careless mistakes or struggling to keep track of your belongings?

Yes, I did. Like I mentioned with my old report cards, making careless mistakes has always been an issue for me. And honestly, it still happens a lot now. 

Um, in my job, even in reports where I know better than to rush, I'll still end up missing a changed date, or I'll transpose a number. Sometimes I'll even leave a placeholder comment right in the workpaper by accident. It's really embarrassing, to be honest, because paying attention to detail is supposed to be my main strength as an auditor, but I just keep making those little errors.
